# Add `value_to_metric` field to include descriptor values in metrics

## Summary

This particular PR right here goes right ahead and adds in a brand new optional field, one that is called `value_to_metric` (and which comes along with a default value of `false`), and it goes and adds this new field onto each and every single one of the descriptors that happen to be present within the rate limit configuration. In the case where this field has been enabled, then what it actually goes on to do is to include the descriptor's own runtime value directly within the metric key itself, and, importantly, it manages to do this even in those cases where the descriptor value happens to have not been explicitly defined anywhere at all within the configuration itself. This here is exactly the thing that ends up providing proper and full visibility into all of the various different rate limit scenarios that there are, and, moreover, it manages to do all of this without there being any need whatsoever to go and pre-define each and every single one of the possible values well ahead of time.

## Problem

The particular way in which things happened to work previously, before all of this, was such that, whenever a given descriptor matched up against some value that had not been explicitly defined within the configuration (that is to say, in the case where it matched by way of a default key that did not have any value attached to it), then the metric key would only ever go and include the descriptor key its own self, and it would not go and include the actual runtime value at all. The net effect of what this ended up doing was to make it quite genuinely difficult to properly track, and to then go on to analyze, the rate limiting metrics for each of the different runtime values, at least without going and making use of `detailed_metric`, which is the very thing that goes and includes the values for absolutely all of the descriptors there are and, as a direct result of doing that, can end up leading to a situation of high cardinality.

## Solution

The brand new `value_to_metric` field is precisely and exactly the thing that goes right ahead and allows the users themselves to selectively go and include the runtime values right into the metric keys, and, importantly, to go about doing so for only the specific descriptors that they themselves happen to actually choose to do it for. This here is exactly what ends up providing a genuinely granular level of fine control over the whole matter and question of the metric cardinality, while, at the very same time as all of that, it still nevertheless manages to properly maintain full and complete visibility into those particular descriptor values which happen to be the ones that are genuinely the important and meaningful ones to actually have on hand for observability purposes.

## Behavior

- **Default behavior**: In that particular case where `value_to_metric` happens to have been set to the value `false` (which is, of course, the default value that it takes on) or else where it has simply not been set at all in the very first place, then the behavior of the whole thing remains entirely, totally, and completely unchanged from the way that it always was before this — which is to say that the descriptors that happen to end up being matched by way of the default keys are only ever going to go and include the key name its own self within the metrics, and nothing more than that.

- **With `value_to_metric: true`**: In that particular case where this has been enabled on some given descriptor, the following behaviors apply:
  - If it so happens that the descriptor ends up matching by way of a default key (that is to say, in the situation with no explicit value being present at all within the config), then the runtime value is going to be the thing that gets itself included right within the metric key, and it does so in just exactly the following sort of manner: `domain.key_value.subkey`
  - If, on the other hand, it instead so happens that the descriptor ends up matching by way of an explicit key+value pairing, or else alternatively by way of a wildcard, then in that case the runtime value is one that is always going to end up being included, no matter what the circumstances happen to be
  - In that particular case where this is combined right together with wildcard matching, then it is going to be the **full runtime value** that ends up getting itself included in the end, and it is very much not going to be merely just the wildcard prefix all on its own by itself

- **Precedence**: In that one particular case where `detailed_metric: true` happens to have been the thing that was set on a given descriptor, then it is going to be the one that goes right ahead and takes full precedence over everything else, and so, as a direct consequence of that, `value_to_metric` ends up simply just being ignored entirely and completely for that one particular descriptor in question (and this whole thing here is something that is done quite deliberately and on purpose, specifically in order to properly maintain the backward compatibility of the whole system).

## Example

**Configuration:**
```yaml
domain: domain
descriptors:
  - key: route
    value_to_metric: true
    descriptors:
      - key: http_method
        value_to_metric: true
        descriptors:
          - key: subject_id
            rate_limit:
              unit: minute
              requests_per_unit: 60
```

**Requests:**
- `route=api`, `http_method=GET`, `subject_id=123` → Metric: `domain.route_api.http_method_GET.subject_id`
- `route=web`, `http_method=POST`, `subject_id=456` → Metric: `domain.route_web.http_method_POST.subject_id`

**Without `value_to_metric`**, both requests would use: `domain.route.http_method.subject_id`

## Changes

### Code Changes
- Added a brand new `ValueToMetric bool` field, going right ahead and placing it over onto the `YamlDescriptor` struct, which is the place where it now lives on as one part of it going forward from here on out
- Added `value_to_metric` in over to the `validKeys` map, and this one particular thing right here was done quite specifically for the sake of, and in direct support of, the whole of the YAML validation process that ends up happening on the configuration
- Added a `valueToMetric bool` field over onto the `rateLimitDescriptor` struct as well, and this here was done quite specifically in order to be able to properly keep track of the flag its own self, doing so on a per-descriptor basis, one single descriptor at a time as they come
- Updated the `loadDescriptors` function in such a way and to such a degree that it now goes right ahead and stores away the `value_to_metric` flag right within each and every one of the descriptor nodes themselves at the point as they are being loaded up
- Updated the `GetLimit` function in such a way that it now goes right ahead and builds out a `value_to_metric`-enhanced version of the metric key, doing exactly so in each and every single case where the flag happens to have been enabled on it
- Handled the whole wildcard matching case as well, doing so specifically so as to properly include the full runtime values in that particular situation where `value_to_metric` happens to have been enabled on the descriptor

### Tests
- Added in a whole set of comprehensive unit tests, ones that go on to properly cover each and every single one of the following particular things in turn:
  - The basic functionality of the whole thing, tested out together with the runtime values being in place
  - The default key behavior, exactly and precisely as it happens to work when together with `value_to_metric`
  - A mid-level descriptor case, once again exactly as it happens to work when together with `value_to_metric`
  - The backward compatibility of it all (that is to say, in the particular case where there is no flag whatsoever being set at all)
  - The interaction that it happens to have with `detailed_metric` (namely, the whole matter and question of the precedence that exists between the two of them)
  - The configured descriptor values, exactly and precisely as they happen to work when together with `value_to_metric`
  - The wildcard matching case, yet once again exactly as it happens to work when together with `value_to_metric`
- Every single last one of these tests goes on to pass successfully, without any failures at all whatsoever appearing anywhere along the way

### Documentation
- Updated the README.md file, and went ahead and did so with each and every single one of the following particular things in turn:
  - Added `value_to_metric` over into the descriptor list definition format there, so that from now on it happens to be properly and fully documented right there in that spot for everyone to see
  - Added in a brand new section entirely of its very own, one that goes by the particular title of "Including descriptor values in metrics", and which then goes on from there to properly explain the whole of the feature itself in full and complete detail
  - Added in Example 10 as well, which is the particular example that goes on to demonstrate the actual real-world usage of it, and it does exactly so together with both the basic scenarios on the one hand and also, alongside them, the wildcard scenarios on the other hand
  - Updated the Table of Contents accordingly (and do please take careful note right here that this one particular thing is going to end up requiring you to go and run `doctoc` in order to properly regenerate the whole thing)

## Testing

Every single one of the existing tests goes on to continue to pass exactly as it should, and this here is precisely the very thing that ends up ensuring that the backward compatibility is properly maintained throughout. The brand new tests that were added then go on from there to verify each and every one of the following particular things in turn:
- ✅ The basic `value_to_metric` functionality works exactly as it should be expected to work
- ✅ The default key behavior correctly goes and includes the values in that one particular case when it has been enabled by the user
- ✅ The wildcard matching case correctly goes and includes the full runtime values, as intended
- ✅ There is genuinely and truly no regression at all whatsoever in that particular case where the flag is simply just not set
- ✅ There is correct precedence properly maintained together with `detailed_metric` in place
- ✅ The whole thing works properly and correctly together with the configured descriptor values as well, just as it ought to

## Backward Compatibility

This particular change right here is one that happens to be fully, entirely, and completely backward compatible in every respect:
- The default value for it is set to be `false`, and so, as a direct result of that particular fact, any and all of the existing configurations that happen to already be out there are simply just going to continue right on to work in exactly the very same way as they always did do before, entirely and totally unchanged in every way
- It only ever goes and affects the metric keys themselves and nothing else, and, even then, it only ends up doing so in that one particular case where it has actually been explicitly enabled by the user in question
- It does not go and change the actual rate limiting behavior its own self in any way, shape, or form whatsoever at all — the one and only single thing that it actually ends up changing, at the end of the day, is simply and solely just the metric naming and nothing more

})

### Context

This particular feature request right here goes right ahead and offers up a brand new AWS check, one that happens to go by the name of `rds_instance_extended_support`. What it is that this new check actually does, at its very core, is to go along and check whether or not the various Amazon RDS DB instances there are happen to be currently enrolled into the Amazon RDS Extended Support program. In the particular event that it turns out to be the case that the instance in question is reporting its own value for `EngineLifecycleSupport` as being set to `open-source-rds-extended-support`, then what that ends up meaning is that it is indeed enrolled, and so, as a direct and immediate consequence of exactly that, the check its very own self will go ahead and fail; otherwise, in any and all of the other cases that there might happen to be, the check will simply just go right ahead and pass instead.

### Description

## Summary

Fixes #3972

The `no-duplicate-selectors` rule will now correctly go and detect duplicate class selectors in the case where they happen to use different CSS escape sequence formats. As an example of this, `.u-m\00002b` and `.u-m\+` are now recognized as being duplicates of one another, and this is because both of them actually represent `.u-m+`.

## Changes

- Added a `normalizeNodeEscaping()` helper over in `normalizeSelector.mjs`, one which makes use of postcss-selector-parser's getter/setter behavior in order to normalize the CSS escaping
- Added some test cases specifically for the escaped selector duplicates

## How it works

The fix leverages the built-in value getter/setter behavior that postcss-selector-parser provides for the ClassName nodes. The getter goes and returns the unescaped value, while the setter, for its part, re-escapes that value into a normalized form instead. So, simply by going ahead and doing `node.value = node.value`, we go and trigger this whole normalization process, which is what then ensures that equivalent selectors will end up comparing as equal to each other, regardless of what their original escape format happened to have been.

Reference: https://github.com/postcss/postcss-selector-parser/blob/1b1e9c3bc10ccc3bc5f07a987caa7f2684c0b52f/src/selectors/className.js#L13-L28

### Context

This particular change here goes ahead and adds in a brand new security check, one that is specifically for the case of GCP Compute Engine, and the whole entire job and purpose of this new check is to go and ensure that the custom disk images are not, under any circumstances, being publicly shared out with anyone at all. The underlying reason that this whole thing genuinely matters so much is the fact that images which have ended up being publicly shared are, as a consequence of that, able to go and end up exposing sensitive data of one kind or another, or otherwise proprietary software of some sort, or even quite specific and revealing infrastructure details, and, worse still than all of that, to go and do all of that exposing directly to unauthorized users who should never have had any access at all, which is precisely the sort of thing that ends up creating some genuinely significant and serious security risks in the process along the way.

### Description

What it is that this PR actually does is go right ahead and add in a brand new GCP check, one whose entire purpose is to verify whether or not the Compute Engine custom disk images happen to have any IAM bindings sitting on them at all that would end up having the overall effect of granting some form of public access to them. The way that the check goes about operating is that it goes right through and very carefully evaluates each and every single one of the custom images that there happen to be, and then, once it has finished doing that, it goes on from there to report right back the following particular set of results:

* **PASS**: the image in question here is not, in any way at all, being publicly shared out with anyone whatsoever
* **FAIL**: the image in question here is in fact being publicly shared out, and specifically it is being shared with `allAuthenticatedUsers`

**Note**: it is worth pointing out that, according to what the GCP documentation itself has to say on the matter, `allUsers` simply cannot ever actually be granted any roles at all on images, and so, precisely because of that particular fact, only `allAuthenticatedUsers` is the one that ends up actually being checked for here.

#### Changes include:

**Compute Service (`compute_service.py`):**
- Added an `images` list of its very own, one whose whole and entire job it happens to be to go along and store away all of the various custom image data that there happens to be present
- Added in a brand new `_get_images()` method, one that goes right ahead and does each and every one of the following particular things in turn, one after the other: first of all, it goes and lists out every single one of the custom images that there are, and it does that listing specifically by way of making a call to `images().list()`; then, secondly, it goes and retrieves the full IAM policy for each and every individual one of those images, and it does that specifically by way of making a call to `images().getIamPolicy()`; and then, thirdly and finally, it goes ahead and extracts out all of the public members (that is to say, the `allAuthenticatedUsers` entries) from out of the bindings that were retrieved
- Added in a brand new `Image` model as well, one that comes complete with a `public_members` field sitting right there on it, ready and waiting to hold onto that particular data

**New Check (`compute_image_publicly_shared/`):**
- The check logic its very own self, which is precisely the thing that goes along and evaluates the public sharing status for each and every single one of the images in turn
- A Metadata JSON file of its very own, one that comes along complete with proper and appropriate remediation guidance that is included right there inside of it for reference
- A whole set of unit tests as well, ones that go along and thoroughly cover both the case of the images that do have public sharing on them and also, on the other side of things, the case of the images that do not have it

This change deprecates `falcon.testing.redirected`, doing so in favor of the standard library's own `contextlib.redirect_stdout` together with `contextlib.redirect_stderr`.

**Changes:**
- Added a deprecation warning onto `falcon.testing.redirected`, and did this specifically by making use of the `falcon.util.deprecated` helper
- Updated the internal test file (namely the one called `test_cmd_inspect_app.py`) so that it now goes ahead and uses the `contextlib` alternatives instead of what it used before
- This has been scheduled in such a way that the eventual removal will end up happening in Falcon 5.0

**Rationale:**
- The popular pytest framework already goes ahead and captures, and then also suppresses, the output that comes out of the successful tests, and it does this automatically by default without needing to be told
- The stdlib itself already provides the equivalent functionality, doing so by way of both `contextlib.redirect_stdout` and also `contextlib.redirect_stderr`
- It reduces the ongoing maintenance burden that we carry, and it does that by going and removing a utility that had by this point become redundant

### Context

The way that the AWS Bedrock service in Prowler is currently implemented, it only ever goes and fetches the very first page of results, and it does this for both the Guardrails and the Agents. What this particular limitation ends up meaning is that, in any environments that happen to have a large number of these resources in them (that is to say, a number of them which exceeds the default AWS page size that is in effect), Prowler ends up failing to properly detect and to scan all of them, and this failure in turn ends up leading directly to security assessments that turn out to be incomplete.

### Description

This PR goes right ahead and implements proper pagination logic for both of the [list_guardrails](cci:1://file:///prowler/prowler/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service.py:54:4-84:13) and the [list_agents](cci:1://file:///prowler/prowler/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service.py:143:4-177:13) methods, both of which happen to live in [bedrock_service.py](cci:7://file:///prowler/prowler/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service.py:0:0-0:0).

Changes include:
- Updated the [[prowler/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service.py](cci:7://file:///prowler/prowler/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service.py:0:0-0:0)](https://github.com/prowler-cloud/prowler/blob/master/prowler/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service.py) logic so that it now goes and iterates its way through each and every one of the available pages of the results, doing so specifically by using the `nextToken` value that is provided to it by the AWS API.
- Added a brand new unit test file, namely [[tests/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service_pagination_test.py](cci:7://file:///prowler/tests/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service_pagination_test.py:0:0-0:0)](https://github.com/prowler-cloud/prowler/blob/master/tests/providers/aws/services/bedrock/bedrock_service_pagination_test.py), and this was in order to properly verify that the pagination logic does correctly go and collect the resources right across the multiple pages.
- Added some inline documentation over to the code itself, doing so in order to explain the whole pagination flow along with the mechanics of the loop.

### Description

<!-- Please insert your description here and provide especially info about the "what" this PR is solving -->
This particular PR right here goes right ahead and adds in a brand new `coverage.changed` option, and this is one that goes on to allow you to go about the business of running each and every one of the tests while, at that very same time, only going and computing the coverage figures for just those particular files that happen to have actually been changed. This here is something that turns out to be genuinely useful for the case of CI pipelines, specifically the ones that find themselves needing to do the following two things:

1. Run the full test suite to ensure all tests pass
2. Compute coverage only for files changed in a pull request

The way that things happened to work previously, before this whole change, was that doing this used to require you to go and run two entirely separate and distinct commands, and the unfortunate effect that this ended up having was that it went and doubled the overall test execution time that you had to sit and wait through.

Resolves #8747 

<!-- You can also add additional context here -->

### Usage

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      changed: 'HEAD', // or any git ref like 'main', 'origin/main'
    },
  },
})
```

The `changed` option itself is one that goes on to accept each of the following particular kinds of values:
- `'HEAD'` - Compare against the last commit
- `'main'` - Compare against the main branch
- `'origin/main'` - Compare against remote main branch
- Any valid git reference

### Testing Instructions

1. Navigate to the test directory:
   ```bash
   cd test/coverage-test
   ```

2. Create a demo config file `vitest.demo.config.ts`:
   ```typescript
   import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'

   export default defineConfig({
     test: {
       include: ['**/file-to-change.test.ts', '**/math.test.ts'],
       coverage: {
         enabled: true,
         provider: 'istanbul',
         reporter: ['text'],
         reportsDirectory: './coverage-demo',
       },
     },
   })
   ```

3. Run tests **without** the `changed` option:
   ```bash
   pnpm vitest run --config=vitest.demo.config.ts
   ```
   
   **Result:** Coverage includes all files
   ```
   File               | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines |
   -------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|
   All files          |   33.33 |      100 |   33.33 |   33.33 |
    file-to-change.ts |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
    math.ts           |      25 |      100 |      25 |      25 |
   ```

4. Modify `fixtures/src/file-to-change.ts` (make any change)

5. Update config to add `changed: 'HEAD'`:
   ```typescript
   coverage: {
     enabled: true,
     provider: 'istanbul',
     reporter: ['text'],
     reportsDirectory: './coverage-demo',
     changed: 'HEAD', // ← Add this line
   },
   ```

6. Run tests again:
   ```bash
   pnpm vitest run --config=vitest.demo.config.ts
   ```
   
   **Result:** Coverage includes only changed files
   ```
   File               | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines |
   -------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|
   All files          |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
    file-to-change.ts |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
   ```

Note: Both of the two test runs shown here go on to fully execute **all tests** (that is to say, both the `file-to-change.test.ts` file and also the `math.test.ts` file), but, and this is the crucial part of it, the second run of the two only goes on to actually report the coverage specifically for the one single modified file.

To go and restate the whole underlying point of this particular feature once more over again, and to do so quite plainly and simply for the sake of achieving complete and total clarity on the matter: the entire goal that is genuinely being pursued here, at the end of the day, is to make it so that one single solitary test run is somehow able to go and accomplish two entirely separate jobs all at the very same time. On the one hand, that one single run goes and proves quite conclusively that the full and complete test suite does in fact pass exactly and precisely as it is supposed to, and then, on the other hand, at that exact same moment in time, it also goes and reports right back the coverage figures, but scoped right down in such a way that they only ever end up covering those particular files which have actually and genuinely been changed. And the real, tangible, practical benefit of going and arranging things in this one particular way is that it manages to accomplish both of those two distinct jobs together, side by side, and it does so without ever once having to go and run the whole of the entire test suite twice separately over, which is, of course, exactly the wasteful and time-doubling situation that used to be flatly required beforehand under the old way of doing things.

It is perhaps worth spelling out, once again, exactly what the various accepted values for the `changed` option end up meaning in practice. When you go and give it the value `'HEAD'`, then it will go and compare the current state of things against the very last commit that was made. When instead you give it the value `'main'`, then it will go and compare against the main branch itself. When you give it the value `'origin/main'`, then it will go and compare against the remote main branch that lives on the origin. And, beyond just those specific examples, it will happily go and accept any other valid git reference at all that you might care to hand it.

As for the testing instructions that are laid out up above, the whole sequence of steps there is really just there in order to let you go and demonstrate the behavior for yourself, first-hand, with your very own eyes. The idea is that you first go and run the tests once through without the `changed` option being set at all, at which point you will see that the resulting coverage report goes ahead and includes each and every one of the files. Then, after you go and make some change or other to one of the fixtures, and after you go and add the `changed: 'HEAD'` line into the config, you run the very same tests through once again, and this second time around you will see that the resulting coverage report now goes and includes only the single file that you actually went and changed, exactly as intended.

To put a little more emphasis on the motivating scenario that sits behind the whole of all of this: the particular kind of situation that this feature is really and truly aimed at helping out with is that of a CI pipeline, and, more specifically still, the sort of CI pipeline that finds itself needing to go and do two separate things together as one. The first of those two things is that it needs to go and run the full and complete test suite, and it does this precisely so as to be able to properly ensure and to confirm that each and every single one of the tests does, in actual fact, end up passing just as it ought to. The second of those two things is that it needs to go and compute the coverage figures, but to do so only for the particular files that happen to have been changed as part of a given pull request, rather than going and doing it for the entirety of the whole codebase all at once. Before this particular change ever came along, satisfying both of those two separate needs together at once meant that you were effectively forced into running two entirely separate commands, one right after the other, and the direct consequence of being forced to do things that way was that the total amount of time that ended up being spent executing all of the tests was, in effect, doubled, which is quite obviously very far indeed from being ideal in a CI setting, where the total wall-clock time taken genuinely does matter quite a great deal.

## Summary

Fixes #3972

The `no-duplicate-selectors` rule is now able to correctly go ahead and detect the duplicate class selectors in exactly those cases where they happen to make use of different CSS escape sequence formats from one another. As a concrete example of what is meant by this, the two selectors `.u-m\00002b` and `.u-m\+` are now going to be recognized as being duplicates of one another, and the underlying reason for that is because both of them are, in actual fact, representing the very same thing, namely `.u-m+`.

## Changes

- Added in a brand new `normalizeNodeEscaping()` helper function, going ahead and placing it over inside of the `normalizeSelector.mjs` file, and this is a helper which goes ahead and makes use of the particular getter/setter behavior that belongs to postcss-selector-parser, doing so specifically and deliberately in order to be able to normalize the CSS escaping that happens to be present in the selectors
- Added in a whole number of new test cases as well, ones that are there specifically and particularly for the case of the escaped selector duplicates that this is meant to handle

## How it works

The particular way that the fix here goes about working is that it goes and leverages the built-in value getter/setter behavior that postcss-selector-parser happens to have available for the ClassName nodes in particular. The getter, for its own part on its side of things, goes ahead and returns right back the unescaped value, whereas the setter, for its own part on its side of things, goes ahead and re-escapes that same value into a properly normalized form instead. And so, simply by going ahead and doing `node.value = node.value`, what it is that we manage to accomplish is to trigger off this whole entire normalization process, and the net effect that comes out of that is to ensure that any equivalent selectors there may be are going to end up comparing as being fully equal to one another, and, moreover, that this particular fact holds true completely and totally regardless of whatever their own original escape format may happen to have been in the very first place to begin with.

Reference: https://github.com/postcss/postcss-selector-parser/blob/1b1e9c3bc10ccc3bc5f07a987caa7f2684c0b52f/src/selectors/className.js#L13-L28

# Add `value_to_metric` field to include descriptor values in metrics

## Summary

Adds an optional `value_to_metric` field (default: `false`) per descriptor. When enabled, it includes the descriptor's runtime value in the metric key even when that value isn't in the config, giving visibility without pre-defining every value.

## Problem

Previously, when a descriptor matched a value not explicitly defined (a default key without value), the metric key included only the key, not the runtime value. Tracking per-runtime-value metrics was hard without `detailed_metric`, which includes all descriptors' values and can cause high cardinality.

## Solution

`value_to_metric` lets users selectively include runtime values in metric keys for specific descriptors — granular cardinality control while keeping visibility into key values.

## Behavior

- **Default** (`value_to_metric` `false`/unset): unchanged — default-key matches include only the key name.
- **`value_to_metric: true`**:
  - default-key match (no explicit value): runtime value included: `domain.key_value.subkey`
  - explicit key+value or wildcard: runtime value always included
  - with wildcard, the **full runtime value** is included, not just the prefix
- **Precedence**: `detailed_metric: true` wins; `value_to_metric` ignored for that descriptor (backward compatibility).

## Example

**Configuration:**
```yaml
domain: domain
descriptors:
  - key: route
    value_to_metric: true
    descriptors:
      - key: http_method
        value_to_metric: true
        descriptors:
          - key: subject_id
            rate_limit:
              unit: minute
              requests_per_unit: 60
```

**Requests:**
- `route=api`, `http_method=GET`, `subject_id=123` → Metric: `domain.route_api.http_method_GET.subject_id`

**Without `value_to_metric`**: `domain.route.http_method.subject_id`

## Changes

### Code Changes

# Add `value_to_metric` field to include descriptor values in metrics

## Summary

This PR goes ahead and adds a brand new optional field, `value_to_metric` (with a default of `false`), and it adds this to each of the descriptors that are in the rate limit configuration. When this field is enabled, what it does is include the descriptor's runtime value right in the metric key, and it does this even in the case where the descriptor value has not been explicitly defined anywhere in the configuration. This is the thing that ends up providing proper visibility into the various different rate limit scenarios, and it does so without there being any need to go and pre-define each and every possible value ahead of time.

## Problem

The way that things worked previously was that, whenever a descriptor matched against a value that wasn't explicitly defined in the configuration (that is to say, it matched by way of a default key that had no value attached), the metric key would only ever go and include the descriptor key itself, and not the actual runtime value. What this ended up doing was making it quite difficult to properly track and then, following on from that, to analyze the rate limiting metrics for each of the various different runtime values, at least without going and making use of `detailed_metric`, which is the very thing that goes and includes the values for absolutely all of the descriptors there are and, as a direct result of doing that, can end up leading to a situation involving high cardinality of the metrics.

## Solution

The new `value_to_metric` field is the thing that allows users to selectively go and include the runtime values into the metric keys, doing so for only the specific descriptors that they choose. This provides a granular level of control over the metric cardinality, while at the same time still managing to maintain proper visibility into the descriptor values that are important.

## Behavior

- **Default behavior**: When `value_to_metric` is set to `false` (which is the default) or is simply not set at all, the behavior remains entirely unchanged from before — descriptors that are matched by way of default keys will only go and include the key name itself in the metrics.

- **With `value_to_metric: true`**: When this is enabled on a given descriptor:
  - If the descriptor happens to match by way of a default key (that is, with no explicit value present in the config), then the runtime value is included right in the metric key, like so: `domain.key_value.subkey`
  - If instead the descriptor matches by way of an explicit key+value pairing or else a wildcard, then the runtime value is always included
  - When this is combined together with wildcard matching, then the **full runtime value** is what gets included, and not merely just the wildcard prefix on its own

- **Precedence**: In the case where `detailed_metric: true` happens to be set on a descriptor, then it is the one that takes precedence, and so `value_to_metric` ends up being ignored for that particular descriptor (and this is done in order to maintain backward compatibility).

## Example

**Configuration:**
```yaml
domain: domain
descriptors:
  - key: route
    value_to_metric: true
    descriptors:
      - key: http_method
        value_to_metric: true
        descriptors:
          - key: subject_id
            rate_limit:
              unit: minute
              requests_per_unit: 60
```

**Requests:**
- `route=api`, `http_method=GET`, `subject_id=123` → Metric: `domain.route_api.http_method_GET.subject_id`
- `route=web`, `http_method=POST`, `subject_id=456` → Metric: `domain.route_web.http_method_POST.subject_id`

**Without `value_to_metric`**, both requests would use: `domain.route.http_method.subject_id`

## Changes

### Code Changes
- Added a `ValueToMetric bool` field over to the `YamlDescriptor` struct
- Added `value_to_metric` into the `validKeys` map, this being for the sake of the YAML validation
- Added a `valueToMetric bool` field over to the `rateLimitDescriptor` struct, in order to track the flag on a per-descriptor basis
- Updated `loadDescriptors` so that it now stores the `value_to_metric` flag right in the descriptor nodes
- Updated `GetLimit` so that it now builds a `value_to_metric`-enhanced metric key whenever the flag is enabled
- Handled the wildcard matching case so as to include the full runtime values in the situation where `value_to_metric` happens to be enabled

### Tests
- Added a set of comprehensive unit tests, ones that go and cover the following:
  - The basic functionality, tested together with runtime values
  - The default key behavior, as it works with `value_to_metric`
  - A mid-level descriptor, as it works with `value_to_metric`
  - Backward compatibility (that is, with no flag set at all)
  - The interaction with `detailed_metric` (namely, the precedence)
  - Configured descriptor values, as they work with `value_to_metric`
  - Wildcard matching, as it works with `value_to_metric`
- All of the tests pass successfully

### Documentation
- Updated the README.md, and did so with the following:
  - Added `value_to_metric` over into the descriptor list definition format
  - Added a brand new section, titled "Including descriptor values in metrics", which goes on to explain the feature
  - Added Example 10, which demonstrates the usage with both the basic and the wildcard scenarios
  - Updated the Table of Contents (and do note here that this requires you to run `doctoc` in order to regenerate it)

## Testing

All of the existing tests continue to pass, which is what ensures backward compatibility. The new tests go on to verify the following:
- ✅ Basic `value_to_metric` functionality
- ✅ Default key behavior includes values when it is enabled
- ✅ Wildcard matching includes the full runtime values
- ✅ No regression at all in the case where the flag is not set
- ✅ Correct precedence together with `detailed_metric`
- ✅ Works together with configured descriptor values

## Backward Compatibility

This change here is one that is fully backward compatible:
- The default value is `false`, and so any existing configurations will simply continue on to work exactly as before, entirely unchanged
- It only ever affects the metric keys, and only in the case where it is explicitly enabled
- It does not go and change the rate limiting behavior in any way at all — it only changes the metric naming

b6f9e003c95f1880bf079782a720b300f8a4c41c.text: This change is an improvement on the earlier #12105, and the way it improves on it is by taking the shard shape and passing that in as the value of the `previous_chunks` parameter, rather than passing in `chunks` for that purpose the way that it was being done before. The practical result that comes out of making this particular substitution is that the rechunking operation ends up producing chunks that are larger in size, while at the very same time those same larger chunks still manage to remain properly shard-aligned. I want to extend my thanks to @dcherian for taking the time to remind me of the important detail that `auto_chunks` will, in nearly all of the cases that come up in practice, go ahead and concatenate the `previous_chunks` argument that has been handed to it. That said, it is worth being clear and explicit that this is not something which holds true in absolutely every single case that can arise. It is precisely because of that caveat that this change opens up the possibility of ending up with chunks that are shard-misaligned, and this can happen specifically in the scenario where the global configuration goes and declares a memory limit whose value happens to be smaller than the size of the shard. This naturally raises a question worth asking: what is it that we ought to do in the particular situation where there turns out to be direct competition between, on the one hand, the global config, and on the other hand, the shard shape of the zarr array in question? Would it perhaps be an appropriate thing for us to raise an exception at that particular point in time, an exception whose whole and entire purpose would simply be to prompt the user into going ahead and changing their own config accordingly so as to suit the particular situation at hand?

### Description

<!-- Please insert your description here and provide especially info about the "what" this PR is solving -->
This particular PR goes ahead and adds a brand new `coverage.changed` option, one that allows you to go about running all of the tests while, at the same time, only computing the coverage for the files that have actually been changed. This is useful for CI pipelines that need to:

1. Run the full test suite to ensure all tests pass
2. Compute coverage only for files changed in a pull request

The way things were previously, doing this used to require you to go and run two entirely separate commands, and the effect of that was that it ended up doubling the overall test execution time.

Resolves #8747 

<!-- You can also add additional context here -->

### Usage

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      changed: 'HEAD', // or any git ref like 'main', 'origin/main'
    },
  },
})
```

The `changed` option accepts:
- `'HEAD'` - Compare against the last commit
- `'main'` - Compare against the main branch
- `'origin/main'` - Compare against remote main branch
- Any valid git reference

### Testing Instructions

1. Navigate to the test directory:
   ```bash
   cd test/coverage-test
   ```

2. Create a demo config file `vitest.demo.config.ts`:
   ```typescript
   import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'

   export default defineConfig({
     test: {
       include: ['**/file-to-change.test.ts', '**/math.test.ts'],
       coverage: {
         enabled: true,
         provider: 'istanbul',
         reporter: ['text'],
         reportsDirectory: './coverage-demo',
       },
     },
   })
   ```

3. Run tests **without** the `changed` option:
   ```bash
   pnpm vitest run --config=vitest.demo.config.ts
   ```
   
   **Result:** Coverage includes all files
   ```
   File               | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines |
   -------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|
   All files          |   33.33 |      100 |   33.33 |   33.33 |
    file-to-change.ts |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
    math.ts           |      25 |      100 |      25 |      25 |
   ```

4. Modify `fixtures/src/file-to-change.ts` (make any change)

5. Update config to add `changed: 'HEAD'`:
   ```typescript
   coverage: {
     enabled: true,
     provider: 'istanbul',
     reporter: ['text'],
     reportsDirectory: './coverage-demo',
     changed: 'HEAD', // ← Add this line
   },
   ```

6. Run tests again:
   ```bash
   pnpm vitest run --config=vitest.demo.config.ts
   ```
   
   **Result:** Coverage includes only changed files
   ```
   File               | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines |
   -------------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|
   All files          |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
    file-to-change.ts |      50 |      100 |      50 |      50 |
   ```

Note: Both of the test runs go on to execute **all tests** (that is, both `file-to-change.test.ts` and also `math.test.ts`), but, crucially, the second run of them only goes on to report the coverage for the one modified file.

In short, the whole point of this option is to let a single run both prove that the full test suite passes and, separately, report coverage scoped down to only the changed files, all without having to run the tests twice over.

It is worth briefly spelling out what the accepted values mean: giving it `'HEAD'` compares against the last commit, giving it `'main'` compares against the main branch, and giving it `'origin/main'` compares against the remote main branch, while any other valid git reference is accepted too. The testing steps above simply let you see this for yourself: run the tests once without the option and coverage includes every file, then add the `changed: 'HEAD'` line and run again, and coverage now includes only the single file you changed, even though both runs execute all of the tests.

### Context

This adds a brand new security check for GCP Compute Engine, one whose job is to detect any and all VM instances that happen to be configured with multiple network interfaces on them. The concern here, the reason it matters, is that VMs which have multiple NICs are able to act as bridges sitting right between networks that are really and truly supposed to remain fully isolated from one another, and this potentially ends up allowing attackers to move laterally, going from one network segment across to another one.

### Description

This PR goes ahead and adds a new GCP check, one that verifies whether or not the Compute Engine instances happen to have multiple network interfaces that are configured on them. The check goes through and carefully evaluates every single one of the VM instances that there are, and then, once done, it reports back to the user the following set of results:

* **PASS**: the instance in question has just a single network interface on it
* **FAIL**: the instance in question has multiple network interfaces on it (that is to say, 2 or more of them in total)

**Note**: instances that happened to be created by GKE, or else that are being used in the role of network virtual appliances, may quite legitimately and genuinely have a real need for multiple network interfaces on them.

This PR goes ahead and changes the rule so that it will now only go and call `fork` in one of two situations: either if the `*syntax` secondary options happen to be the ones being used, or else if the file that is being linted happens to contain `@property` at-rules that go on to extend the syntax. In any other case at all besides those two, the rule instead just goes and uses the cached lexer that it gets from `context`.

I am going to go ahead and open up an issue in order to remove the secondary options entirely (they are, at this point, now redundant, on account of the fact that we went and added `languageOption`), and the goal of that is so that only the more performant `languageOption` is the one that remains available. That said, it does seem to be the case that forking on any new definitions within a file is something that is simply unavoidable, though.

Benchmarked using our standard config:

```

	extends: ['stylelint-config-standard'],
};

And the cumulative gains combined with https://github.com/stylelint/stylelint/pull/9061:

```

In other words, the core of the change is simply that the rule now avoids the relatively expensive `fork` call in the common case, only paying that cost when the `*syntax` options or `@property` at-rules actually make it necessary, and otherwise reusing the cached lexer — which is exactly what produces the large speed-ups shown in the benchmark numbers above. The thing that this particular PR sets out to do, right at the very heart of it, is to introduce one brand new delimiter keyword argument, taking that argument and going ahead and adding it directly onto the req.get_param_as_list() method as it currently exists.

This particular enhancement that is being made is precisely the thing that ends up making it genuinely possible to go and parse the sort of list-style query parameters which happen to make use of delimiters that are something other than the default comma that would normally be assumed by default (as a few concrete examples of what is meant here, one could point to things such as spaces, or alternatively pipes). The actual splitting logic that is involved in the whole of all of this is something which only ever gets itself applied in the one specific circumstance where the value belonging to the parameter that is in question happens to take on the particular form of a single, lone string all by itself, and it is precisely and exactly this restriction here which is the thing that goes on to serve the purpose of preserving the already-existing behavior of the framework in each of those cases where it finds that it has to handle multiple separate and entirely distinct instances of the very same parameter all appearing together at once within one single query string.

### Context

This adds a brand new security check for GCP Compute Engine, one whose job is to ensure that the custom disk images are not being publicly shared with anyone at all. The reason that this matters so much is that images which have ended up being publicly shared are able to go and end up exposing sensitive data, or proprietary software, or even quite specific infrastructure details, and to do all of that exposing directly to unauthorized users, which is something that goes on to create some genuinely significant security risks.

### Description

This PR goes ahead and adds a new GCP check, one that verifies whether or not the Compute Engine custom disk images happen to have any IAM bindings on them that end up granting public access. The check goes through and evaluates every one of the custom images, and then it reports back the following results:

* **PASS**: the image in question is not being publicly shared with anyone at all
* **FAIL**: the image in question is being publicly shared out with `allAuthenticatedUsers`

**Note**: according to the GCP documentation, `allUsers` cannot actually be granted any roles on images, and so, because of that, only `allAuthenticatedUsers` is the one that ends up being checked here.

#### Changes include:

**Compute Service (`compute_service.py`):**
- Added an `images` list, one that is there to store the custom image data
- Added a `_get_images()` method, one that goes and does the following set of things in turn: it lists out all of the custom images that there are by way of a call to `images().list()`; it then retrieves the IAM policy for each one of the images by way of a call to `images().getIamPolicy()`; and finally it extracts out the public members (that is to say, the `allAuthenticatedUsers`) from out of the bindings that it got back
- Added an `Image` model of its own, one that comes along with a `public_members` field sitting on it

**New Check (`compute_image_publicly_shared/`):**
- The check logic itself, which goes and evaluates the public sharing for each and every image
- A Metadata JSON file, one that comes with remediation guidance included
- Unit tests, ones that go and cover the images both with and without public sharing on them

### Context

This particular change here goes ahead and adds in a brand new security check, one that is specifically and particularly for the case of GCP Compute Engine, and the whole entire job and purpose of this new check is to go and detect any and all of the VM instances that happen to have been configured with multiple network interfaces attached onto them. The real, underlying concern that sits behind the whole of all of this is the fact that VMs which happen to have multiple NICs on them are, precisely as a direct result of that, able to go and act in the capacity of bridges that end up sitting right there in between networks which are genuinely and truly supposed to be kept fully, completely, and properly isolated from one another at all times, and the real danger that comes out of that is that this potentially ends up opening the door to allowing attackers to go and move laterally, making their way from one network segment across and over into another separate one that they were never intended to be able to reach in the very first place at all.

### Description

What it is that this PR actually does is go right ahead and add in a brand new GCP check, one whose entire purpose is to verify whether or not the Compute Engine instances happen to have multiple network interfaces that are configured on them. The particular way in which the check here goes about operating and doing its job is that it goes right through and very carefully and methodically evaluates each and every single last one of the VM instances that there happen to be present, and then, once it has finished up with doing that whole part, it goes on from there to report right back to the user the following particular set of results, and it does so in each and every case that it comes across:

* **PASS**: the instance in question here happens to have only just a single, solitary network interface configured on it, and nothing more than that
* **FAIL**: the instance in question here happens to have multiple network interfaces configured on it (which is to say, a grand total of 2 or more of them all told when they are counted up together)

**Note**: it is genuinely and truly worth taking a moment to bear in mind right here that those instances which happened to have been created by GKE in the first place, or else, as another possibility, instances that are being put to use in the particular role and capacity of network virtual appliances, may in fact quite legitimately, reasonably, and genuinely turn out to have a real and entirely valid need for multiple network interfaces to be present on them.

#### Changes include:

**Compute Service (`compute_service.py`):**
- Added in a `network_interfaces` field onto the `Instance` model, and this particular thing here was done specifically, intentionally, and quite deliberately in order to be able to store all of the network interface data on it going forward from this point onward

**New Check (`compute_instance_multiple_network_interfaces/`)** — this is the brand new check directory that has been added for all of this
